summary: Learners derive the volume formula for a right rectangular prism from its layer structure: with whole-number edge lengths in centimetres, the base layer holds l × w unit cubes (an area of l × w cm²), and the height h tells how many identical layers stack up, so V = l × w × h = base area × height (B × h). The goal is understanding why multiplying three edge lengths counts the cubes, not reciting a string. Learners then apply both V = l × w × h and V = B × h to real contexts (boxes, tanks), estimate, compare volumes, and record answers in cm³ or m³.
misconceptions: Uses V = l×w×h rotely with no sense of layers (Strategy D), so cannot adapt to B×h or explain why it works.
Adds the edge lengths (l+w+h) instead of multiplying, or multiplies only two of the three dimensions.
Confuses volume with surface area, or records cm² instead of cm³.

activities.title: Build the prism layer by layer
steps: Set a box to 4 × 3 × 5 and watch the base layer tile in as 4 × 3 = 12 unit cubes, which cover a base area of 12 cm²; name this base area B.
Stack that identical 12-cube layer upward 5 times to fill the box, tracking the readout as it builds '12 × 5 = 60 cm³' alongside '4 × 3 × 5'.
Change the height from 5 to 10 and predict, then check, what happens to the number of layers and the total volume.
Switch to a tank skin and relate the same count to how much water fills the container.
Re-express the result as B × h and say in words: 'one base layer, repeated so many times high.'
activities.insight: Multiplying the three edge lengths counts cubes because l × w is one layer and h is how many identical layers there are; V = l × w × h is the same idea as V = base area × height.

activities.title: Apply and compare prism volumes
steps: Compute the volume of several labelled cuboids using V = l × w × h, writing the unit as cm³ each time.
Find a missing edge length when given a prism's volume and two of its dimensions.
Given the base area B and height h (instead of three separate edges), compute V = B × h.
Compare two cuboids and decide which holds more, estimating before calculating.
Spot and correct worked examples that add the dimensions (l + w + h) or multiply only two of the three.
activities.insight: The formula is a tool for real problems: you can run it forwards (edges to volume), backwards (volume and two edges to the third), and in the B × h form, and you must use all three dimensions and the cubic unit.

activities.title: Explain why packing equals multiplying
steps: Take a labelled 4 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm cuboid with a real prompt ('a tank 4 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm — how much water fills it?') and find its volume.
In words or on a diagram, reveal the base layer (12 cubes), the number of layers (5), and the product l × w × h, explaining why they match.

Answer the probing questions: Why does multiplying the three edge lengths give the number of cubes? What is the base area, and how many layers high? If the tank were twice as tall, what happens to the volume? Why cm³ and not cm²?
activities.insight: Being able to justify V = l × w × h via base-layer × height — not just produce 60 — is the mark of relational understanding, and it transfers to the B × h form and to real capacity questions.

checkQuestion: Give a labelled cuboid (4 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm) with a real-world prompt ('a tank 4 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm — how much water fills it?'). Say: 'Find its volume, and explain why your method works.' Then WATCH whether they multiply all three dimensions, whether they can connect it to layers (base 12, five layers) or to B×h, and whether they write cm³.
checkAnswer: 60 cm³ = 4 × 3 × 5, explained as a base layer of 12 cubes repeated 5 times (B × h); records the answer in cm³.
